fields.meaning: I humbly state that…, it is because… | As soon as…, depending on…
examples: My father retires next year, but I have a younger brother and sister at home. I am also thinking of cutting back on my part-time job so I can study more. That is why I am applying for a scholarship.
I thought I should at least let you know about that matter, and so I am writing you this letter.
After considering the sales forecast and the costs, we have decided to abandon the development of this product.
Because the person in charge was away, our reply was delayed, for which we sincerely apologize.
Due to various circumstances, it has been decided that the schedule will be changed.
For the reasons stated above, I will not be participating this time.
fields.explain:
Structure: Vます +次第、～
The second clause is usually a clause expressing the speaker's intention or action (contacting, notifying, starting…).
Context: written language/business, polite announcements; rarely used in casual conversation (replaced by ～たらすぐ/～たらすぐに).
Not used when the second clause is a general habit or an obvious fact with no sense of "immediately".

•
Meaning: "As soon as… then…", "once … is done, …". Emphasizes that the two actions follow each other immediately in time.

•
Scope of use: situations where you announce a plan or action that will be carried out as soon as the condition in the first clause is completed.

•
Nuance: formal; common in business emails, service announcements, and promises of action.

•
Meaning frame: [A completed] → (immediately) [do B]. The second clause rarely expresses a vague, prolonged state.
fields.notes:
• Often used with verbs signaling completion: 分かる・判明する・届く・到着する・準備ができる・確認する・決まり次第…
• In emails: "～が分かり次第、ご連絡申し上げます。" is a very common formula.
• On sentence rhythm: put a comma after 次第 to clearly separate the two clauses.
meaning_vi: ～したらすぐに過去形(かこけい)の文(ぶん)にはならない
Immediately after...
examples: 1. 「向こうに着きしだい、電話してください」
Please call me as soon as you get there.
2. 「皆さんがそろいしだい出発しましょう」
Let's leave as soon as everyone is here.
3. 次の会合は来月１日です。場所は決まり次第お知らせします。
The next meeting is on the 1st of next month. We will let you know the venue as soon as it is decided.
mistakes: Wrong nuance: using it in casual conversation → sounds stiff and distant.
JLPT: tricks you with its role as a sentence ending compared with ～というわけです; asks you to choose the pattern that fits a business situation.
Wrong position: placed in the middle of a passage instead of at the end of the summarized content.

rows: Spoken, more neutral; no emphasis on a formal announcement nuance
<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>いたらすぐ<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>して。
Different meaning: a condition that depends on a noun, not "as soon as"
<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>は<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby><ruby>次第<rt>しだい</rt></ruby>で<ruby>変<rt>か</rt></ruby>わる。
Different function: a sentence that explains or wraps up the content
<ruby>以上<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>、ご<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>した<ruby>次第<rt>しだい</rt></ruby>です。

examples: I think we could do it a bit faster depending on how we go about it.
I was told that my salary would go up depending on my performance.
Depending on your effort, your life can change dramatically.
Depending on how you explain it, the other person may react better too.
We will adjust the scale of the plan depending on the funds.
Depending on the weather, the event may be moved indoors.
fields.explain:
Structure: N +次第で／次第では／次第に
"次第で" states a relationship of dependence; "次第では" states a possibility in a particular case.
The second clause is usually a verb expressing change (変わる・左右される・決まる・調整する…).
Often used with general nouns:努力・考え方・状況・予算・天気・使い方・対応・方針…

•
Meaning: the result or outcome depends on the factor N (a condition, circumstance, way of doing something, point of view, etc.).

•
Focus: a conditional cause-and-effect relationship; things change according to N.

•
Nuance: neutral and logical; can be used in both spoken language and written language.
fields.notes:
• N + 次第で emphasizes the decisive "lever": the factor N is the variable that governs the result.
• 次第では often goes with a clause stating a possible choice or option: 中止する／延期する／見送る…
• A natural contrasting pair: 「能力・努力・工夫」⇄「結果・成果・評価」. | Sentence-final form: ～次第だ (depends on)
mistakes: Wrong meaning: taking ～次第で as "as soon as" → confusing it with ～次第 (Vます+次第).
Wrong part of speech: putting a verb before 次第で → it must be noun + 次第で.
JLPT: often tests the distinction between ～によって／～いかんで（は）／～次第で in terms of formality.

rows: Broader meaning; leans toward "by way of/thanks to/done by"
<ruby>国<rt>くに</rt></ruby>によって<ruby>文化<rt>ぶんか</rt></ruby>が<ruby>違<rt>ちが</rt></ruby>う。
More formal; common in stiff written texts
<ruby>成績<rt>せいせき</rt></ruby>いかんでは<ruby>進学<rt>しんがく</rt></ruby><ruby>不可<rt>ふか</rt></ruby>。
Different meaning: a time relationship, not dependence on a condition
<ruby>準備<rt>じゅんび</rt></ruby>ができ <ruby>次第<rt>しだい</rt></ruby><ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>。

fields.meaning:
①～であるば（仮定(かてい)、条件(じょうけん)）
Assumption, condition, as long as | Within the scope of…, as long as…
examples: As long as we keep quiet, nobody will find out this secret.
As long as you are a student, you have to follow the school rules.
As long as he doesn't make any big mistakes, Murayama will surely win.
"Unless something serious comes up, I will attend."
This cough won't stop unless you quit smoking. Please take this opportunity to try to quit.
As far as I know, that is the fastest way to get there.
fields.explain: ◎ An expression of limitation meaning " if the condition is met", " within that scope".

examples: As long as you keep working hard, you won't get fired.
As long as you live in a city, a certain amount of noise can't be helped.
Unless it rains or something, we will go hiking as planned.

〈インタビュー：　最高齢の選手の話〉
As long as my stamina holds out, I want to keep doing my best.
fields.explain: ◎ Expresses the idea "if a certain condition is satisfied".

fields.connection: V volitional form + か + Vる・Vます + まいか
examples: I still can't decide whether to attend the party or not.
I've been gaining too much weight lately, so I can't decide whether to eat the cake or not.
fields.explain: ◎ Expresses hesitation about whether or not to do an action.
fields.notes:
Taken from (Speed Master); fuller 接続 (まいか attaches to Vる or Vます depending on the verb group). meaning_vi: whether to ～ or not ⏐ explain: Used in written language.
Formal sentence. ⏐ examples: 1. 本当のことを話そうか話すまいか迷った、結局全部話した。
I hesitated over whether to tell the truth or not, but in the end I told everything.
2. 食べたいけど、太りたくないし、食べようか食べまいか考えているところです。
I want to eat it, but I don't want to gain weight, so I'm thinking about whether to eat it or not.

examples: Today it's been nothing but meetings since the morning.
He is dressed in black from head to toe.
This investment offer sounds like nothing but good things, but you need to be careful.
The new system is nothing but rules, and it's suffocating.
This week has been nothing but work, and I haven't had time to rest.
His speech was nothing but bragging, and I got sick of it.
fields.explain:
Attaches directly after a noun; often used with の when it modifies another noun:黒ずくめの男.
Used for a sense of "all one color" or "densely packed" rather than simply quantity.
Often used in advertising and journalism to emphasize "completeness".

• "All/full of/covered entirely by …": emphasizes singleness, uniformity, all one color.
• Often used with colors, repeated events, rules, and things that are entirely good or bad.
• Nuance: can be positive (いいことずくめ) or negative (苦情ずくめ／規則ずくめ).
• Different from づくし: ずくめ = one kind covering everything; づくし = "all kinds within one theme".
fields.notes:
• Fixed color phrases: 黒ずくめ／白ずくめ（all black/all white）.
• With prolonged events: ～三日間ずくめで（nothing but … for 3 days）.
• Avoid using it for objects covered in dirty material → まみれ is more suitable.
mistakes: Used with a verb: ×勉強ずくめする → correct: 勉強ずくめの日々.
Confused with づくし: ずくめ = one color; づくし = all kinds within one theme.
Using ずくめ for dirt or for being covered in a substance is the wrong nuance → use まみれ.

rows: <ruby>間違<rt>まちが</rt></ruby>いだらけのレポート。
Covered all over (with a substance), negative
All dishes/all kinds within a theme
<ruby>野菜<rt>やさい</rt></ruby>づくしのコース。

examples: The meeting will be held in Osaka.
Applications are accepted via the web form.
Today's business hours end at 5 p.m.
We will send you the details by email.
With this, I declare the ceremony closed.
Exchanges at our store require a receipt.
fields.explain:
Degree of formality: high; used in announcements, invitations, event posters, and internal documents.
Spoken replacements: で/に (place/point in time) and で/により (means).
Often used with:開催・実施・受け付ける・行う・終了・販売・配布・連絡・案内.
Position: mid-sentence (NにてV), or at the beginning of a sentence in fixed phrases (これにて、以上にて...).
Avoid it in everyday conversation; prefer で/に to sound natural.

• Indicates the place where something happens: equivalent to で in spoken language. Example: 東京にて開催する。
• Indicates the ending/starting point in time (announcements): 10時にて終了。
• Indicates means/method: 電話にてお問い合わせください。 (equivalent to で/により)
• Formal nuance; used a lot in announcements, correspondence, and corporate/government documents.
• Not used for the destination of movement (× 東京にて行く), but for the place where an event or action takes place.
• Compared with において: において is more academic/general; にて leans toward practical announcements (events, sales, reception...)
fields.notes:
• Very frequent in documents: event posters, business emails, store announcements.
• "NにてのN" is mostly seen in writing; in speech it usually becomes "NでのN".
• Not combined with verbs of motion indicating a destination (行く・来る) in the destination sense.
• Polite expressions that often go with it: 〜いたします、〜しております、〜させていただきます。 explain: Often used on notice boards or in letters…
Formal sentence. ⏐ examples: 1. 現地にて解散となります。
We will disperse on site.
2. 電話カメールにてご連絡ください。
Please contact me by email or phone.
3. 京都にて　洋子より（*旅先からのハガキの最後などでよく使う）
From Yoko, in Kyoto.
mistakes: Wrongly used for a destination: × 東京にて行く → ◯ 東京にて開催する／東京へ行く。
Overusing it in everyday conversation makes sentences stiff; change it to で/に.
Confused with において in abstract scope: 教育にて × → 教育において。
Point in time: 10時にて終了 (announcement) is natural; in speech, 10時で終了 is usually used.

rows: Natural, less formal than にて
<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>で<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>う。
<ruby>教育<rt>きょういく</rt></ruby>において<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>だ。
Emphasizes the agent/cause; にて leans toward formal means
<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>により<ruby>受<rt>う</rt></ruby>け<ruby>付<rt>つ</rt></ruby>ける。
As of the end of, by means of
More formal when saying "ends as of ..."
<ruby>本日<rt>ほんじつ</rt></ruby>をもって<ruby>終了<rt>しゅうりょう</rt></ruby>。
Fixed phrase for closing a speech
これにて<ruby>閉会<rt>へいかい</rt></ruby>。

examples: The success or failure of this project depends on fundraising.
Whether I can go on to the next level of school depends on the results of the final exams.
Hiring depends on the person's character and aptitude.
Whether the negotiations continue depends on the other party's response.
fields.explain:
Often used in affirmative sentences that set rules or give an overall evaluation.
Not used in everyday casual speech; replaced by "〜による/〜次第だ".
Suitable when you want to single out the "deciding factor" in an objective way.

• "~のいかんだ" = "depends on ~ / is decided by ~".
• Emphasizes that N is the factor that determines result X. Highly formal; often seen in official documents.
• "いかん" is a Sino-Japanese noun (如何) meaning "degree/condition/state (how good or bad)".
• Only combines with nouns (努力・資金・成否・態度・結果・審査 等). Does not attach directly to adjectives/verbs.
fields.notes:
• "いかん" often goes with abstract nouns: 成否・可否・結果・状況・態度・出来（でき）など.
• Because it is highly formal, it suits announcements, regulations, and contracts.
• In legal/administrative discourse, "〜のいかんにかかわらず／問わず" appears very often.
mistakes: Used directly with an adjective/verb: ×速いのいかんだ → 速さのいかんだ (convert to a noun).
Using it in casual conversation sounds stiff and unnatural; use による/次第だ instead.
Confusing its function with "では/によっては" (conditional variants) → "のいかんだ" only states a general relationship of dependence.

rows: Very formal; states a deciding relationship
<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>のいかんだ
Due to, because of, depending on
<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>は<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>による
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>君<rt>きみ</rt></ruby><ruby>次第<rt>しだい</rt></ruby>だ
Sets a condition to state a consequence
<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>のいかんでは<ruby>処分<rt>しょぶん</rt></ruby>も
N のいかんにかかわらず
<ruby>年齢<rt>ねんれい</rt></ruby>のいかんにかかわらず

examples: Tea without sugar, please.
I read a book in a park with no one around.
Don't be misled by groundless criticism.
It is an unprecedented challenge.
Please refrain from visiting without prior notice.
fields.explain:
Put N1 before のない to emphasize "what is lacking".
More formal than "N1抜きのN2" (N1 intentionally left out) and "N1なしのN2" (without N1 in general).
Often used in legal documents, announcements, and academic writing.

• Modifier form: "N2 that has no N1", "N2 not accompanied by N1", equivalent to "N2 without N1".
• Expresses absence (of something material or abstract: 根拠, 前例, 予告, 音, 人影…).
• More formal/written than ～なしの/～抜きの in some contexts.
fields.notes:
• N1 is a noun; if it is a quality expressed by a na-adjective or い-adjective, it is usually nominalized: 可能性のない, 安全性のない.
• Common phrases: 前置きのない, 合意のない, 許可のない, 音のない（無音の）.
• In formal headlines, "前例のない" is very common to emphasize that something is unprecedented.
mistakes: Wrong order: ×ないのN → correct: NのないN.
Mixed up with なしの/抜きの: なしの is neutral, 抜きの emphasizes "intentional removal".
Using のない with a verb → incorrect: the concept must be nominalized (例: 許可のない撮影).
JLPT: choose correctly when saying "groundless/unprecedented": 根拠のない／前例のない are common answers.

rows: <ruby>根拠<rt>こんきょ</rt></ruby>のない<ruby>噂<rt>うわさ</rt></ruby>
<ruby>砂糖<rt>さとう</rt></ruby>なしのコーヒー
アルコール<ruby>抜<rt>ぬ</rt></ruby>きのパーティー

examples: Starting with Tokyo, cherry blossoms are reaching full bloom in many places.
Many people involved attended, starting with the company president.
It is highly regarded in Asian countries, Japan first and foremost.
It is popular with a wide range of age groups, starting with elementary school children.
When it comes to environmental problems, there is a lot we can do, starting with saving electricity in our daily lives.
fields.explain:
Placed at the beginning of a sentence to lead into a broader scope.
More formal than "〜をはじめ," but with the same basic meaning; choose according to the context.
N must be a typical/representative member of a larger set.
Often used with nouns for place names, job titles, groups of people, and items.

• "Starting with N, including others of the same kind."
• Emphasizes the starting point/typical case (N) and then extends to a broader scope.
• Style of official information: speeches, reports, news articles.
fields.notes:
• In local news reports: 地名 + をはじめとして/に is very common.
• When N is a superior (社長・校長), it creates a respectful, polite nuance.
• Not used for a complete listing; implies there are many other members. meaning_vi: First and foremost, ～ ⏐ explain: Gives one main example, then lists other similar examples. ⏐ examples: 1. 会議には中国をはじめ、アジアの国々が参加した。
Asian countries, starting with China, took part in the conference.
2. わが国では、野球をはじめとして、サッカーやテニスなど、様々なスポーツがさかんである。
In our country, many sports are popular, starting with baseball, as well as soccer and tennis.
mistakes: Confused with "〜をはじめに(して)": that one indicates a sequence, "starting with ... first".
Used when there is no broader scope: × 社長をはじめとして、社長が来た。
Choosing a non-representative subject: using an N that is too small or isolated is unnatural.

rows: Noun modifier "including N first and foremost ..."
<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>をはじめとする<ruby>国々<rt>くにぐに</rt></ruby>
<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>などで<ruby>人気<rt>にんき</rt></ruby>
Written language, emphasizes "the leader"; strong nuance
<ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>筆頭<rt>ひっとう</rt></ruby>に〜

examples: Asian countries, led by Japan, took part.
It has been decided that the executives, starting with the president, will attend.
Demand for mobile devices, such as smartphones, is growing.
Tourist spots in the Kansai region, such as Kyoto, are bustling in spring.
I'm good at science subjects, especially math.
International organizations, including the WHO, issued a statement.
fields.explain:
Placed right before the head noun N2 to modify it directly.
Formal tone; suitable for informational, academic, and journalistic texts.
Make sure there is a set relationship: N1 is a member of the set N2.
Not used when N2 has only one member; it must be a group/set.

• Used like an attributive adjective to describe a set N2 in which N1 is the representative/leading member.
• Formal nuance; often appears in articles, presentations, and reports.
• N1 and N2 must belong to the same semantic field (the same kind): country–countries, person–group of people, product–products...
fields.notes:
• Headline pattern: 「N1をはじめとするN2、〜」 is very common.
• Often combined with words denoting a set: 国々／関係者／製品群／都市／機関／科目.
• A long complement can be inserted after N2 and the sentence still stays formal and coherent.
mistakes: Wrong category relationship: × 日本をはじめとするヨーロッパ → Japan is not part of Europe.
N2 is not a set: × 日本をはじめとする文化 → N2 should be a countable set: 文化圏／文化行事.
Confused with "〜をはじめに(して)": a pattern about the order of actions, with a completely different meaning.

<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>をはじめとして、〜
